Triggers.value: Visible injuries or wounds on others

Maladaptive Strategies.value: try hard not think about the trauma
I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied

Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
I should have protected others and I failed

issues.explanation: Pain Recall implies the patient personally sustained bodily injury during the trauma, which is hard to reconcile with the trauma type being trauma to a loved one unless there was also direct physical injury to the patient. That is not otherwise supported by the profile.

Physical Vulnerability and permanent bodily damage imply the patient believes his own body was physically harmed. For a trauma-to-a-loved-one presentation, this is difficult to explain clinically without evidence that he was also directly injured.

Military Topics is a trigger that suggests a military/combat-linked trauma context, but no other trigger, memory, threat, or appraisal item supports a military-related formulation. As a standalone item it feels disconnected from the rest of the profile.

Avoid Driving is plausible for motor-vehicle trauma, but here it lacks support from the trauma type and from the rest of the profile. With no transport-related trigger or memory content, it appears to target a symptom domain not otherwise represented.

For trauma to a loved one, visible injuries is a plausible trigger, but darkness and alcohol smell are not well anchored to the rest of the profile. Nothing in memory, threat, or appraisals suggests a dark-space or alcohol-related trauma context, so these triggers feel disconnected rather than part of a coherent loved-one trauma presentation.

Avoiding work/study is hard to reconcile with this patient's occupation as a paramedic unless the trauma is clearly tied to the workplace, but the rest of the profile frames the trauma as harm to a loved one rather than occupational trauma. Drug use is also insufficiently supported elsewhere in the profile: there are no other items indicating broad externalising coping or substance-related trigger context, making this strategy feel tacked on.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study
issues.explanation: Self-blame can occur after trauma to a loved one, but this specific wording implies a direct causal role in the event. The rest of the profile does not provide supporting content suggesting he believes his own actions caused the loved one's trauma. The other appraisals are about damage and unreliability of self, so this item is the least integrated with the stated trauma type and surrounding node content.

Alcohol smell is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only trigger that suggests a substance-related context. The other trigger and memory items center on victims/injuries, which fits a paramedic exposed to injured loved ones or victims. Without any corresponding memory, threat, or appraisal content linked to alcohol, this item stands out as weakly connected to the rest of the trauma representation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Drug Use: take drugs
issues.explanation: Drug use can occur in PTSD, but here it is the only maladaptive strategy that implies substance misuse. The rest of the profile emphasizes work avoidance, suppression, sensory reliving, and hypervigilant threat responses. With no parallel alcohol/substance-related trigger, appraisal, or memory content, this item looks clinically disconnected from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, self-blame is plausible only if the patient had a clear perceived role in failing to protect or respond. In this profile, the other items describe reliving of victims/injuries, hypervigilance, and damaged-self beliefs, but nothing else indicates a responsibility-based trauma narrative. This makes the specific self-blame item the least coherent appraisal relative to the rest of the selected content.

vignette:
Tariq Nasser is a 40-year-old Lebanese-American paramedic who has worked emergency medical services in a mid-sized Midwestern city for fourteen years. He is married, the father of two school-aged children, and by all outward measures had been, until eighteen months ago, someone his colleagues described as steady under pressure - the kind of person you wanted in the back of the rig when things went badly wrong. That steadiness is what makes his current state so disorienting to him. He presents to the clinic quietly, choosing a chair with its back to the wall and a clear sightline to the door before he has said a single word.

The event that brought Tariq here involved his younger brother, Samir, who was involved in a serious road traffic collision on a Sunday afternoon last spring. Tariq was off duty, but the call came through a mutual friend who had witnessed the accident, and Tariq arrived at the scene before the ambulance. What he found - Samir pinned in the driver's seat, a deep laceration across his forearm exposing tissue beneath, blood pooling on the door panel - was something Tariq's professional training had prepared him to manage in strangers. It had prepared him for nothing when the face looking up at him was his brother's. He worked on Samir with his hands, applying pressure, talking to him, doing what he knew to do, and Samir survived. But in those minutes on the roadside, Tariq had been certain, with a completeness he had never felt before, that his brother was going to die in his arms.

In the weeks that followed, Tariq found that the memory returned without warning and without mercy. When it came back, it did not arrive as a recollection - it arrived as an event happening now, complete with the smell of blood mixed with something chemical from the ruptured engine, the exact weight of Samir's arm under his hands, the sound of traffic still moving on the adjacent lane. The terror he had felt on that roadside was indistinguishable from the terror he felt sitting at his kitchen table. There are portions of that afternoon he cannot account for at all - a gap between the moment he knelt down and the moment he heard the ambulance siren - and this absence frightens him in its own particular way, as though something important happened that he is being denied access to.

At work, the trouble became concrete and unavoidable. Tariq is a paramedic, which means that visible wounds on patients are not occasional encounters but the core material of his days. A laceration on a patient's arm, the antiseptic smell that hits him the moment he wheels a gurney through the emergency department bay, a colleague's offhand mention of a victim's age or appearance - any of these can collapse the distance between the present call and that Sunday afternoon. He began calling in sick on shifts when he could, and when he could not avoid going in, he found himself throwing himself into administrative tasks, restocking, training paperwork - anything that kept him moving and occupied without requiring him to be present with an injured patient. His supervisor has noticed. Two colleagues have asked whether he is all right. The gap between who Tariq was at work and who he is now has become visible to people around him, and this visibility is its own source of distress.

At home he sits with his back to walls. He startles badly when his wife touches his shoulder from behind, a reaction that has left her confused and, on one occasion, tearful. He cannot hold a thought through to its end. He has come to believe, with a quiet and settled certainty, that something in him broke that afternoon and has not repaired - that the man who could be counted on, by his brother, by his crewmates, by his own family, no longer exists in any reliable form. He had been there, trained, present, and still he had felt helpless. That feeling has not left him.

What finally brought Tariq to seek help was a conversation with Samir, who is fully recovered and bewildered by his brother's withdrawal. Tariq could not explain to Samir why he had been avoiding his calls. He sat with the phone in his hand afterward and understood that he was losing things he could not afford to lose. He comes to the clinic hoping, cautiously, to find some way back. What he fears most is that there is no way back - that this is simply who he is now.
